What my screens are doing to me: an observational log

Ashlee Shum

The question I started asking myself

I am a final year Computer Science student, which means I’m going to be looking at screens for the rest of my life. This project gave me an excuse to actually measure what I’d been suspecting for a while: that “media” is no longer something I do, it’s something I’m always inside.

So for over two weeks I logged every meaningful media session, built on top of the previous observational log for project 2. I recorded what it was, how long it lasted, what time of day, what I was using it for, on what device, and how it left me feeling. The result is the small dataset behind this story, and the five plots below.

Where my screen time actually goes

For my first plot, I visualised how much time I spent on each respective media type.

Bar chart showing total minutes per media type across the observation period. Each bar is labelled with its total in minutes, and the categories are sorted from most to least time consumed.

The result was unflattering but unsurprising: short-form video (TikTok and Instagram) absorbs more of my time than any other category, even though each individual session feels small. The “just 10 more minutes” of scrolling really do add up. Reading, the category I say I value most, sits noticeably lower than I’d hoped.

How my media habit moves through the fortnight

The next question was about patterns - are there any I can see across the days?

Daily timeline showing total minutes of media consumption per day as purple bars, with a dashed darker line marking the overall daily mean across the observation period.

The bars show the daily total, and the dashed line is the mean minutes per day across the whole fortnight. The mean line gives me an honest indicator of how much time I actually spend consuming media.

We can see that as time passes, the time I spend on media also increases. This may be due to burnout, or becoming less busy due to university work or holidays.

Note: there is a period of time where I didn’t log any data, as that was the time we had project 3.

When does each kind of media take over?

This is the plot that truly humbled me.

Faceted bar chart with one panel per time of day (Morning, Afternoon, Evening, Late night). Each panel shows the number of logged sessions for each media type, ranked from highest to lowest.

Each kind of media has its own time slot. TikTok and Instagram dominate the late night panel, the “just five more minutes” trap. Reading, when it happens, happens primarily in the morning. All the other categories are superseded by social media… the doom scroll.

Each session, and the average for its purpose

This plot is two layers in one frame.

Jittered dot plot showing the duration of every individual session, grouped by the purpose I logged for it. A purple triangle marks the mean session length within each purpose category.

Each small dot is one logged session, scattered along the horizontal axis by how many minutes it lasted. The dark triangle in each row is the mean session length for that purpose. Sessions logged as Education tend to be short but consistent as the dots somewhat cluster, and the triangle is pulled forward. Entertainment sessions are longer on average and far more spread out. Knowing the average without seeing the spread would have given me data that is easily misinterpreted.

How does media leave me feeling?

For this project I added a “How did you feel after?” question. The fifth plot pulls out the words that appeared most across those mood entries.

Bar chart of the top five words across all mood responses, each bar labelled with its count.

The dominant words say more about my media consumption than any minute count could. Drained and guilty show up disproportionately, and almost always next to late-night short-form sessions. Inspired and energised are rarer but tied tightly to deliberate, daytime use. The takeaway: the way I feel after media has less to do with the content and more to do with whether I chose it.

So what?

Doing this project changed how I look at my phone, and really showed me how the minutes add up. What was useful was being forced to log before I could plot, and noticing the choice in real time, several times a day, for two weeks.

If you’re reading this, I hope you take this as a sign to reconsider your screen time, and how it may be affecting you.
